families.name: Temporal Inconsistency Detection
families.definition: Methods that detect deepfake videos by analyzing spatial and temporal inconsistencies, such as motion artifacts or frame-to-frame discrepancies, that arise from the generation process.

properties.text: These methods leverage the fact that current generation techniques struggle to maintain temporal coherence across adjacent frames.
They utilize 3D CNNs, recurrent networks, or specific modules to capture local motions and inter-frame inconsistencies.
This approach is effective for video data where static frame-based analysis may miss dynamic artifacts.
Some variants focus on specific cues like co-motion patterns or optical flow to identify unnatural movements.

limitations.text: Performance can degrade if the forgery method successfully generates temporally coherent videos.
These methods are generally not applicable to single-image forgery detection.
They may be sensitive to video compression and quality variations that obscure subtle temporal artifacts.

families.name: Frequency Domain Analysis
families.definition: Detection techniques that exploit artifacts in the frequency domain, such as phase spectrum changes, DCT anomalies, or high-frequency noise patterns, to distinguish real from synthetic media.

properties.text: These methods identify that GANs and other generators leave specific traces in the frequency space that are often invisible in the spatial domain.
They utilize filters, Fourier transforms, or wavelet analysis to extract discriminative features from amplitude and phase spectra.
Frequency-based cues are often more robust to certain types of spatial manipulations and compression than raw pixel values.
Some approaches use shallow learning or specific filter banks to capture these spectral discrepancies.

limitations.text: High-quality compression can significantly degrade or remove these frequency artifacts.
The specific frequency traces may vary between different generative models, limiting generalization.
These methods may struggle with images that have undergone significant post-processing or resizing.

families.name: Biological and Physiological Signal Detection
families.definition: Approaches that detect deepfakes by analyzing physiological signals, such as heart rate variations via remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) or eye-blinking patterns, which are often absent or unnatural in synthetic videos.

properties.text: These methods rely on the premise that synthetic faces do not naturally exhibit biological rhythms like blood flow or spontaneous blinking.
They analyze subtle color changes in skin or specific facial movements to infer physiological states.
This approach provides a distinct signal from visual artifact-based methods, potentially offering better robustness to visual quality changes.
Some methods use neural ODEs or attention mechanisms to model these biological signals.

limitations.text: These signals are only available in video data, not static images.
The presence of these signals depends on the quality of the source video and the specific generation method used.
Advanced generation models may eventually learn to simulate these physiological cues, rendering the method obsolete.

families.name: Audio-Visual Consistency Detection
families.definition: Methods that detect deepfakes by evaluating the synchronization and semantic alignment between the audio track and the visual facial movements, such as lip-sync accuracy.

properties.text: These approaches hypothesize that manipulation of either modality leads to dissonance or mismatch between audio and visual content.
They utilize multi-modal networks to compare features from audio and video streams, often using contrastive learning or similarity scores.
This method is particularly effective for talking-head videos where lip movements should correspond to speech phonemes.
Some techniques specifically look for phoneme-viseme mismatches or affective cue inconsistencies.

limitations.text: This method is inapplicable to silent videos or images without an audio track.
High-quality lip-sync generation models can produce highly consistent audio-visual pairs, reducing detection accuracy.
It may fail if the audio and video are manipulated independently but remain semantically plausible.

families.name: Generalization and Domain Adaptation
families.definition: Strategies aimed at improving the robustness of detectors to unseen forgery methods, compression artifacts, or domain shifts through techniques like contrastive learning, knowledge distillation, and meta-learning.

properties.text: These methods address the problem of catastrophic forgetting and poor generalization to new datasets or generation models.
They employ self-supervised learning, adversarial training, or domain adaptation to learn invariant features across different domains.
Some approaches use knowledge distillation to transfer detection capabilities from high-quality to low-quality compressed images.
Contrastive learning is used to create embeddings that are sensitive to diverse forgery types rather than specific artifacts.

limitations.text: These methods often require complex training pipelines or large amounts of diverse data.
Generalization to completely novel, unseen generation architectures remains a significant challenge.
Performance may still degrade under extreme compression or adversarial perturbations.

families.name: Transformer-Based Detection
families.definition: Detection frameworks that utilize Vision Transformers (ViT) or attention mechanisms to capture global context and long-range dependencies in images or videos for forgery detection.

properties.text: These methods overcome the limited receptive field of CNNs by modeling pairwise interactions between image patches.
They are effective at capturing global inconsistencies and subtle manipulation traces that local CNN filters might miss.
Some architectures combine RGB features with high-frequency or noise features in a multi-modal transformer setup.
Attention mechanisms allow the model to focus on specific regions of interest for localization tasks.

limitations.text: Transformer models can be computationally expensive compared to lightweight CNNs.
They may require large datasets to train effectively due to the number of parameters.
Performance on low-resolution or heavily compressed images may be limited if the patch size is not optimized.

families.name: GAN Attribution and Fingerprinting
families.definition: Techniques that identify the specific generative model (e.g., StyleGAN, ProGAN) that produced a fake image by learning model-specific fingerprints or artifacts.

properties.text: These methods treat detection as a multi-class classification problem to attribute images to their source GAN.
They exploit unique statistical properties or structural artifacts left by specific GAN architectures.
Some approaches use open-set recognition to handle images generated by unseen models.
This provides more granular information than simple real/fake classification, aiding in forensic investigation.

limitations.text: Attribution is difficult for images generated by private or modified models not seen during training.
The fingerprints may be removed or altered by post-processing operations like JPEG compression.
The method is limited to GAN-generated content and may not apply to other generative paradigms like diffusion models.

families.name: Image Manipulation Localization
families.definition: Methods that not only detect the presence of forgery but also localize the specific tampered regions within an image using segmentation masks or attention maps.

properties.text: These approaches use fully convolutional networks or U-Net architectures to predict pixel-level masks of manipulated areas.
They often combine detection and localization in a multi-task learning framework.
Some methods use graph-based representations or similarity networks to identify inconsistent regions.
This provides explainability by showing exactly where the manipulation occurred.

limitations.text: Localization is more challenging than binary classification and requires precise ground-truth masks for training.
Performance degrades significantly with compression and resizing, which blur the boundaries of tampered regions.
It is difficult to localize forgeries that involve subtle, global changes rather than localized splicing or copy-move.

families.name: Face Swapping and Reenactment Generation
families.definition: Generative models and techniques used to create deepfakes by swapping identities, reenacting expressions, or animating faces, which serve as the source of the forgeries to be detected.

properties.text: These methods include GANs, autoencoders, and neural radiance fields (NeRFs) for high-fidelity face synthesis.
They aim to preserve identity, expression, and pose while transferring attributes from a source to a target.
Recent advances focus on real-time performance, high resolution, and disentanglement of identity and motion.
Understanding these generation methods is crucial for identifying the artifacts they leave behind.

limitations.text: These are offensive tools in the context of security, though they are essential for creating training data for detectors.
High-fidelity methods can produce results that are visually indistinguishable from real videos, challenging detection.
Some methods require specific conditions, such as aligned faces or specific lighting, to work optimally.

families.name: Controllable Image Editing and Manipulation
families.definition: Generative frameworks that allow users to edit images based on text, sketches, or semantic attributes, which can be used for benign purposes or to create sophisticated forgeries.

properties.text: These methods use latent space manipulation, diffusion models, or GAN inversion to modify specific parts of an image.
They enable fine-grained control over attributes like hair, expression, or background while preserving identity.
Text-guided methods leverage CLIP or similar models to align visual changes with natural language descriptions.
These tools are increasingly accessible and can be used to create realistic but misleading media.

limitations.text: The ease of use lowers the barrier for creating malicious content.
The resulting edits can be very realistic, making them hard to detect with traditional artifact-based methods.
Controllability often comes at the cost of fidelity or may introduce subtle artifacts in unedited regions.
Generalizing detectors to unseen forgery methods and generation models remains a significant challenge.
Detecting high-quality, low-compression deepfakes that lack obvious visual artifacts is difficult.
Developing robust methods that withstand adversarial perturbations and post-processing operations like JPEG compression is an ongoing issue.
Creating interpretable and explainable detection methods that provide visual evidence for their decisions is an active area of research.
Efficiently detecting deepfakes on edge devices or in real-time applications with limited computational resources is a practical constraint.
Attributing fake images to specific generative models, especially private or unseen ones, is not yet fully solved.
Handling the lack of large-scale, diverse, and high-quality datasets for training robust detectors is a persistent problem.
